set.t: The 1899 'Baty found it' rumour is answered by his 1900 return: three digs (1874, 1899, 1900) found nothing. The 1874 confession is second-hand. City park and Coast Guard ground: look-only. An 1879 newspaper 20 ft down means the sand has moved: a shifting dune can bury a cache far deeper than it was laid, or carry it off the summit. The sums grow with each retelling: several thousand dollars in 1899, gold and diamonds in 1900, $40,000 in 1903, $30,000 in 1913. The 1913 'base of the hill, between two pines' version and Baty's crest shaft point to different parts of the same dune. On lidar the dune foot is 120-250 m from the crest to the N and S, inside the ring, but 430-650 m out to the E, SW and W, outside it.

tw-mi-grand-haven-light-house-hill-convi.st: A 1913 Detroit Free Press feature names the convict as William Jenkins, jailed by Gray for horse stealing in Civil War days and later given life at Joliet for a bank robbery. Dying of tuberculosis, he told Gray that he and two others had brought $30,000 in gold from a western bank job by way of Milwaukee and buried it at the base of Five-Mile Hill between two pines, and he drew a map. Lumbermen cut the pines, and Gray dug for weeks. The feature calls Baty 'Ichabod Beattie', a Pueblo miner with a metal 'indicator', and says his shaft went 95 ft. Later seekers included James O'Connell and John Luiken, and in 1921 the Tribune said someone dug into the hill 'every decade'.
src: Detroit Free Press, 23 Nov 1913, p. 69, 'Stranger May Still Hear Story of a Buried Treasure at the Foot of Five-Mile Hill in Ottawa; One Man Dug Down 95 Feet' (Newspapers.com 1048465948)
